## Where This Fits
The second week of Part III. Of the six places a capability can come from (the table from W1), five have been ticked; the remaining one — **knowledge retrieved from outside the model** — opens this week. Three earlier results are used directly. W1: a language model compresses a distribution, not a set of propositions, and even perfectly clean training data leaves a floor under the hallucination rate (Kalai & Vempala). W5: not every token placed in the context is actually used. W11: every token in the context has a price — compute to read it, and then its KV entries are read again for every token written.

**The context is the only place where what a model "knows" can be changed without touching its weights.** The question for the week follows: for each answer, which tokens should go in, who chooses them, and when the answer is wrong, how do we find out which step failed? There are seven questions; the first three are about *finding* and the last four about *using*.

**First, why keep knowledge outside the weights?** Facts stored in weights have three structural limits. Updating them requires retraining (W8: new facts are learned slowly, and learning them raises hallucination). They carry no pointer to a source. And the long tail is not learned: whether a model can answer a factual question is tied to how often the fact appeared in its pre-training data (Kandpal et al., ICML 2023). For rare entities, scaling the model up barely helps, whereas adding retrieval does; for popular entities, retrieval can turn a correct answer into a wrong one (Mallen et al., ACL 2023). Retrieval is therefore not a gain in every case, and the condition under which it helps can be written down.

**Second, three ways of scoring.** A retriever does one thing: it assigns a score to a (question, passage) pair. The methods differ in *when the question and the passage meet*. BM25 lets them meet only at the level of words; it needs no training and is the most reliable method for exact strings. A bi-encoder compresses each side into one vector, and the two meet in a single inner product — which is why the passage side can be computed in advance and indexed. Late interaction keeps one vector per token; the two sides meet later, and the index is an order of magnitude larger. A cross-encoder reads the two sides together; it is the most accurate, cannot be precomputed, and is used only to re-rank a few candidates. This comparison is the most important table of the week, and it is the table of W6 once more: a state of fixed size against a state that grows with length.

**Third, who defines "similar"?** A bi-encoder is trained with a contrastive loss whose optimum is a probability ratio. The score measures how strongly a passage and a question occur together among the training pairs, and the choice of negative examples decides what counts as dissimilar. This is the conclusion about word2vec from W1, returning with larger consequences. How many different notions of relevance one vector can hold has a computable lower bound (Weller et al., ICLR 2026, this week's reading). With documents as simple as "Jon likes quokkas and apples" and queries as simple as "who likes quokkas?", the best embedding models reach less than 20% recall@100 on a corpus of 50,000 documents, while BM25 is almost perfect. The explanation is still disputed — a preprint from November 2026 argues that dimensionality is not the main cause — and both positions are presented. Leaderboards have been optimised against as well: on RTEB (2026), which keeps part of its test data private, the ranking of models correlates with the public leaderboards at only 0.38.

**Fourth, which step failed?** End-to-end accuracy combines three quantities: whether the evidence reached the context, the probability of a correct answer when it did, and the probability of a correct answer when it did not. One number cannot locate a problem; three can. The condition under which retrieval helps, the reason a larger top-$k$ is not always better, and the question of where to cut a document into chunks can all be read from this one expression.

**Fifth, a citation is not evidence that the source was used — this week's failure case.** In the answers of generative search engines, only about half of the sentences are fully supported by their own citations (Liu et al., Findings of EMNLP 2023). Even when a cited passage does support the sentence, the model may have answered from memory first and attached a passage that happens to agree (Wallat et al., ICTIR 2025, the second half of this week's reading). This is the mistake of W3 (attention weights) and W10 (chain-of-thought) in the form it takes this week: a readable intermediate product taken for the mechanism. W14 closes that line of argument with SAE features.

**Sixth, now that contexts can be very long, is retrieval still needed?** Putting every document into the context gives better answers on average and costs far more (Li et al., EMNLP 2024 industry track). The two approaches give the same answer on more than 60% of questions, so the sensible design routes each question to one of them instead of choosing one for all. With the two roofs measured last week, this trade-off can be worked out on the blackboard. The failure of long contexts has also been restated: what hurts is less the length than material that resembles the evidence and competes with it for attention.

**Seventh, who decides what to look up?** One retrieval followed by one generation is the simplest arrangement. Letting the model decide whether to search, what to search for, and when it has enough is agentic retrieval, and the reinforcement learning of W9 can train exactly this behaviour (Search-R1). One level further out, retrieval is only one answer to the question "what should the model see at this step?" The system prompt, tool descriptions, conversation history and notes all compete for the same budget; since 2025 this has been called context engineering. Retrieved text is read by the model as if it could contain instructions, which is where next week begins.

**The side-by-side comparison of the three scoring methods (with BM25 written live), the measurement of the three-term decomposition, and the test "remove the cited passage — does the answer change?" are run by the instructor on the demo machine.** The corpus is this course's own published website and slides, whose rehearsal measurements are in no model's weights. Students run nothing. For chunking and query rewriting, a few controlled comparisons appeared in 2026; their conclusions contradict one another and depend on the corpus. The evaluation of RAG still has no agreed standard. The week says so plainly.

## Learning Objectives
1. State the three structural differences between parametric and non-parametric knowledge (cost of updating, traceability, coverage of the long tail); write the marginalisation in which RAG treats the retrieved passage as a latent variable; and use the condition $a_{+} > a_{0}$ to judge whether retrieval will help on a given class of questions.
2. Write BM25 and say which failure each of its three parts repairs (IDF, saturation of term frequency, length normalisation). Compare BM25, the bi-encoder, late interaction and the cross-encoder by *when the question and the passage meet*, and derive from that their costs (whether anything can be precomputed, the size of the index, the number of model calls per question) and their failure modes.
3. Derive from InfoNCE that the optimal score is a probability ratio (with in-batch negatives, the pointwise mutual information of question and passage); explain how the sampling of negatives changes what "similar" means, and connect this to the result for SGNS in W1. Explain why unlabelled positives among the hard negatives push correct passages away.
4. Derive on the blackboard the lower bound on the dimension of single-vector retrieval, $d_{\text{e}} \ge \log\binom{n}{k} / \log(1 + 1/\gamma)$, and say why it is a lower bound and a loose one. Describe the design and the result of LIMIT, and compare the two explanations on offer (too few dimensions; a mismatch between embedding similarity and task relevance): what each predicts, and which experiment separates them.
5. Write the three-term decomposition $P(C) = r\,a_{+} + (1 - r)\,a_{0}$ and read from it the marginal value of better retrieval, the interior optimum of top-$k$, and the $r^{m}$ of questions that need several pieces of evidence. Design a failure-attribution procedure for a RAG system: measure $r$, $a_{+}$ and $a_{0}$ separately, then split "wrong" into answering wrongly and failing to abstain.
6. Distinguish citation correctness (the cited passage supports the sentence) from citation faithfulness (the sentence was written because of that passage); design an intervention that measures the latter; and place it on the critical line that runs through attention weights, chain-of-thought and citations.
7. Use the ledger of W11 to estimate, for the demo machine, the time and memory of "everything in the context" against "a thousand retrieved tokens". Explain why the KV cache of a prefix can be reused while the KV caches of arbitrary passages cannot simply be concatenated. Summarise the empirical comparison of long context and retrieval (average quality, cost, the share of identical answers) and the routing approach.
8. Explain which failures of single-shot retrieval are addressed by iterative and agentic retrieval and how that behaviour can be trained (special tokens for self-critique; reinforcement learning with a verifiable reward). Give an operational definition of context engineering (choosing and maintaining the tokens placed in the window at each step), and say why retrieved text is an attack surface.

## References
- **Textbooks**: **JM3** (release of 2026-08-19), Vol. II ch. 11 *Information Retrieval and RAG* — information retrieval first and RAG second, the same order as the first half of this week (the chapter title was checked; the sections were not checked one by one). **HOLLM** ch. 8 *Semantic Search and RAG* (the clearest visual and hands-on treatment; its notebooks are written for Colab). Neither book covers the second half of the week (the three-term decomposition, citation faithfulness, the cost of long contexts, context engineering); for that half the material is the papers below and the instructor's notes.

**Why keep knowledge outside the weights**
- Lewis et al., **Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks**, NeurIPS 2020 (arXiv:2005.11401) — the source of the name; treats the retrieved passage as a latent variable and marginalises over the top $k$; trains the query encoder jointly with the generator
- Khandelwal et al., **Generalization through Memorization: Nearest Neighbor Language Models**, ICLR 2020 (arXiv:1911.00172) — kNN-LM: interpolates the model's own distribution with one built from nearest neighbours in a datastore, with no further training; the abstract reports a 2.9-point drop in perplexity on Wikitext-103
- Izacard & Grave, **Leveraging Passage Retrieval with Generative Models for Open Domain Question Answering**, EACL 2021 (arXiv:2007.01282) — Fusion-in-Decoder: each passage is encoded separately and the decoder attends to all of them — an alternative to plain concatenation
- Kandpal et al., **Large Language Models Struggle to Learn Long-Tail Knowledge**, ICML 2023 (arXiv:2211.08411) — the abstract: the ability to answer a factual question tracks the number of relevant documents seen in pre-training; closing the long tail by scaling alone would take many orders of magnitude
- Mallen et al., **When Not to Trust Language Models: Investigating Effectiveness of Parametric and Non-Parametric Memories**, ACL 2023 (arXiv:2212.10511) — PopQA; on rare entities retrieval beats models orders of magnitude larger, while on popular entities unassisted models remain competitive — hence retrieving only when needed
- Kalai & Vempala, **Calibrated Language Models Must Hallucinate**, STOC 2024 (arXiv:2311.14648) — cited in W1: the statistical floor under hallucination; the starting point of this week

**Four ways of scoring**
- Robertson & Zaragoza, **The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond**, *Foundations and Trends in Information Retrieval* 3(4), 2009 (DOI 10.1561/1500000019) — the standard reference for BM25: from the probabilistic model of retrieval to the formula
- Karpukhin et al., **Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering**, EMNLP 2020 (arXiv:2004.04906) — the reference bi-encoder trained with in-batch negatives
- Khattab & Zaharia, **ColBERT: Efficient and Effective Passage Search via Contextualized Late Interaction over BERT**, SIGIR 2020 (arXiv:2004.12832) — late interaction and MaxSim; Table 4: a 154 GiB index for MS MARCO
- Santhanam et al., **ColBERTv2: Effective and Efficient Retrieval via Lightweight Late Interaction**, NAACL 2022 (arXiv:2112.01488) — the abstract: residual compression shrinks the index by a factor of 6–10
- Nogueira & Cho, **Passage Re-ranking with BERT**, arXiv:1901.04085 (2019) — where cross-encoder re-ranking starts; **preprint**
- Formal, Piwowarski & Clinchant, **SPLADE: Sparse Lexical and Expansion Model for First Stage Ranking**, SIGIR 2021 short paper (arXiv:2107.05720) — a learned sparse representation: keeps the inverted index and lets a model set term weights and add terms that do not occur
- Thakur et al., **BEIR: A Heterogenous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models**, NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Benchmarks (arXiv:2104.08663) — zero-shot evaluation on 18 datasets: BM25 is a robust baseline, and re-ranking and late interaction do best on average at a high computational cost; **models of 2021**
- Cormack, Clarke & Büttcher, **Reciprocal Rank Fusion Outperforms Condorcet and Individual Rank Learning Methods**, SIGIR 2009, pp. 758–759 (DOI 10.1145/1571941.1572114) — RRF: fuses two retrievers using ranks alone
- Malkov & Yashunin, **Efficient and Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Using Hierarchical Navigable Small World Graphs**, *IEEE TPAMI* 42(4), 2020 (arXiv:1603.09320) — HNSW; the trade-off among recall, latency and memory in approximate nearest-neighbour search
- Douze et al., **The Faiss library**, arXiv:2401.08281 (2024) — an overview of vector-index designs; **preprint**
- Chen et al., **M3-Embedding: Multi-Linguality, Multi-Functionality, Multi-Granularity Text Embeddings Through Self-Knowledge Distillation**, Findings of ACL 2024 (arXiv:2402.03216) — BGE-M3: one backbone that outputs dense, sparse and multi-vector representations

**Who defines "similar"**
- van den Oord, Li & Vinyals, **Representation Learning with Contrastive Predictive Coding**, arXiv:1807.03748 (2018) — the source of InfoNCE; the optimal scoring function is proportional to a density ratio; **preprint**
- Wang & Isola, **Understanding Contrastive Representation Learning through Alignment and Uniformity on the Hypersphere**, ICML 2020 (arXiv:2005.10242) — the two things a contrastive loss does: pull positives together and spread all points apart
- Xiong et al., **Approximate Nearest Neighbor Negative Contrastive Learning for Dense Text Retrieval**, ICLR 2021 (arXiv:2007.00808) — ANCE: mines hard negatives with the current index
- Qu et al., **RocketQA: An Optimized Training Approach to Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering**, NAACL 2021 (arXiv:2010.08191) — the introduction: of the top-retrieved passages not labelled positive in MS MARCO, a manual check found 70% to be positives — mining hard negatives also mines unlabelled positives
- Steck, Ekanadham & Kallus, **Is Cosine-Similarity of Embeddings Really About Similarity?**, Companion Proceedings of the ACM Web Conference 2024, pp. 887–890 (arXiv:2403.05440) — an analytical result for linear models: the choice of regularisation alone can make cosine similarities arbitrary
- Ethayarajh, **How Contextual are Contextualized Word Representations? Comparing the Geometry of BERT, ELMo, and GPT-2 Embeddings**, EMNLP 2019 (arXiv:1909.00512) — cited in W1: contextual representations are not isotropic — another reason to read cosine similarities with care
- Weller et al., **On the Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-Based Retrieval**, ICLR 2026 (arXiv:2508.21038) — **this week's reading (in full)**: a lower bound on the dimension of single-vector retrieval (a sphere-packing argument with a margin), the critical $n$ found by optimising free embeddings, and the LIMIT dataset; read the ICLR version (arXiv v2), whose theory differs from v1
- Archish et al., **Beyond Dimensionality: Domain Shift and Catastrophic Forgetting in Single- vs. Multi-Vector Retrieval**, arXiv:2603.29519 (v2, 2026-11) — a rebuttal of the previous paper; the abstract: $2k + 1$ dimensions suffice in principle, and the main causes are domain shift and a mismatch between embedding similarity and task relevance; fine-tuning recovers LIMIT at the price of severe forgetting, much less so for multi-vector models; **preprint**
- Reimers & Gurevych, **The Curse of Dense Low-Dimensional Information Retrieval for Large Index Sizes**, ACL 2021 (arXiv:2012.14210) — the abstract: as the index grows, dense representations degrade faster than sparse ones; the lower the dimension, the more false positives
- Kusupati et al., **Matryoshka Representation Learning**, NeurIPS 2022 (arXiv:2205.13147) — the leading coordinates of one vector can be used on their own: dimension becomes an adjustable knob
- Wang et al., **Text Embeddings by Weakly-Supervised Contrastive Pre-training**, arXiv:2212.03533 (2022) — E5; the abstract claims the first model to beat BM25 on BEIR without labelled data; **preprint**
- Wang et al., **Improving Text Embeddings with Large Language Models**, ACL 2024 (arXiv:2401.00368) — embedding models built on an LLM backbone, trained on data synthesised by an LLM
- Zhang et al., **Qwen3 Embedding: Advancing Text Embedding and Reranking Through Foundation Models**, arXiv:2506.05176 (2025) — **a technical report**; embedding and re-ranking models at 0.6B, 4B and 8B, with dimensions 1,024, 2,560 and 4,096, which accept a task instruction; this week's demos use the 0.6B models
- Weller et al., **FollowIR: Evaluating and Teaching Information Retrieval Models to Follow Instructions**, NAACL 2025 (arXiv:2403.15246) — the abstract: existing retrieval models fail to make correct use of instructions attached to a query
- Su et al., **BRIGHT: A Realistic and Challenging Benchmark for Reasoning-Intensive Retrieval**, ICLR 2025 Spotlight (arXiv:2407.12883) — 1,384 real queries for which finding the relevant document requires reasoning; the abstract: models that lead the leaderboards perform poorly here

**Evaluating embeddings**
- Muennighoff et al., **MTEB: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark**, EACL 2023 (arXiv:2210.07316) — the standard leaderboard for text embeddings
- Enevoldsen et al., **MMTEB: Massive Multilingual Text Embedding Benchmark**, ICLR 2025 (arXiv:2502.13595) — more than 500 tasks in over 250 languages; **the one to use for multilingual and Traditional Chinese retrieval**
- Verma et al., **RTEB: An Overfitting-Resistant Benchmark for Embedding Model Evaluation**, NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track (<https://neurips.cc/virtual/2026/poster/139103>) — 48 retrieval datasets, 28 of them private; the abstract: the ranking of twenty models has a Spearman correlation of only 0.38 with BEIR and MTEB

**Which step failed**
- Barnett et al., **Seven Failure Points When Engineering a Retrieval Augmented Generation System**, CAIN 2024 (arXiv:2401.05856) — an experience report from three deployed systems: seven failure points (missing content, missed top-ranked documents, not in context, not extracted, wrong format, incorrect specificity, incomplete); **an experience report, not a controlled study**
- Chen et al., **Benchmarking Large Language Models in Retrieval-Augmented Generation**, AAAI 2024 (arXiv:2309.01431) — RGB: splits what RAG demands of a model into four abilities — robustness to noise, rejecting when it should, integrating several sources, and robustness to counterfactuals; in English and Chinese
- Liu et al., **Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts**, *TACL* 2023 (arXiv:2307.03172) — covered in W5; this week deals with its consequences for RAG
- Cuconasu et al., **The Power of Noise: Redefining Retrieval for RAG Systems**, SIGIR 2024 (arXiv:2401.14887) — the abstract: highly ranked passages that are related but do not contain the answer harm generation, whereas random documents do not have this effect
- Yoran et al., **Making Retrieval-Augmented Language Models Robust to Irrelevant Context**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2310.01558) — irrelevant context can turn correct answers into wrong ones; trains the model to ignore it
- Jin et al., **Long-Context LLMs Meet RAG: Overcoming Challenges for Long Inputs in RAG**, ICLR 2025 (arXiv:2410.05983) — as the number of retrieved passages grows, accuracy rises and then falls; the stronger the retriever, the sharper the fall (hard negatives)
- Joren et al., **Sufficient Context: A New Lens on Retrieval Augmented Generation Systems**, ICLR 2025 (arXiv:2411.06037) — separates questions by whether the context is sufficient; the abstract: when it is not, large models often answer wrongly instead of abstaining
- Longpre et al., **Entity-Based Knowledge Conflicts in Question Answering**, EMNLP 2021 (arXiv:2109.05052) — substitutes entities in the passage to see whether the model follows its memory or the passage — one origin of the "edit" intervention
- Xie et al., **Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth: Revealing the Behavior of Large Language Models in Knowledge Conflicts**, ICLR 2024 Spotlight (arXiv:2305.13300) — the abstract: models readily follow external evidence that is coherent and convincing even when it conflicts with their memory, yet favour the evidence that agrees with memory when both kinds are present
- Yang et al., **CRAG -- Comprehensive RAG Benchmark**, NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks (arXiv:2406.04744) — the abstract: most advanced LLMs reach at most 34% accuracy on their own, and adding RAG in a straightforward way raises this only to 44%

**Chunking and query formulation (controlled studies exist; consensus does not)**
- Chen et al., **Dense X Retrieval: What Retrieval Granularity Should We Use?**, EMNLP 2024 (arXiv:2312.06648) — indexing by "propositions" instead of passages improves both retrieval and downstream QA
- Günther et al., **Late Chunking: Contextual Chunk Embeddings Using Long-Context Embedding Models**, arXiv:2409.04701 (2024) — embeds the whole document first and pools per chunk afterwards, so that each chunk carries its context; **preprint**
- Anthropic, **Introducing Contextual Retrieval**, an Anthropic **post**, 2024-09-19 (<https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval>) — **a company post, not peer-reviewed**; an LLM writes one sentence of context for each chunk before indexing; self-reported retrieval failure rate 5.7% → 3.7%, and 1.9% with BM25 and re-ranking added
- Bennani & Moslonka, **A Systematic Analysis of Chunking Strategies for Reliable Question Answering**, arXiv:2601.14123 (2026) — **a three-page preprint**; SPLADE with an 8B generator on Natural Questions: overlap brings no measurable benefit, and sentence chunking is the most cost-effective
- Shaukat, Adnan & Kuhn, **A Systematic Investigation of Document Chunking Strategies and Embedding Sensitivity**, arXiv:2603.06976 (2026) — **preprint**; 36 chunking methods × 6 domains × 5 embedding models, with relevance judged by an LLM: content-aware chunking clearly beats fixed-length splitting
- Śmigielski et al., **Chunking Methods on Retrieval-Augmented Generation - Effectiveness Evaluation Against Computational Cost and Limitations**, KES 2026 (arXiv:2606.00881) — the abstract: newer chunking methods are tailored to particular data, with limited evidence across scenarios; **the conclusions of these three studies do not agree**
- Gao et al., **Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels**, ACL 2023 (arXiv:2212.10496) — HyDE: an LLM first writes a hypothetical answer, which is then used as the query
- Ma et al., **Query Rewriting for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models**, EMNLP 2023 (arXiv:2305.14283) — rewrites the query before retrieving

**A citation is not evidence of use**
- Liu, Zhang & Liang, **Evaluating Verifiability in Generative Search Engines**, Findings of EMNLP 2023 (arXiv:2304.09848) — a human audit of four generative search engines: on average 51.5% of sentences are fully supported by their citations, and 74.5% of citations support the sentence they are attached to
- Gao et al., **Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations**, EMNLP 2023 (arXiv:2305.14627) — ALCE: a benchmark for generation with citations, with automatic citation precision and recall
- Wallat et al., **Correctness is not Faithfulness in RAG Attributions**, ICTIR 2025, pp. 22–32 (arXiv:2412.18004) — **this week's reading (§4–§5)**: separates citation correctness from citation faithfulness; an experiment designed to expose post-rationalisation finds up to 57% of citations unfaithful (one model, under deliberately constructed conditions)
- van Dort & Heuss, **How Do LLMs Cite? A Mechanistic Interpretation of Attribution in Retrieval-Augmented Generation**, ECIR 2026, LNCS 16485, pp. 458–473 (arXiv:2606.28358) — activation patching on Llama-3.1-8B locates the components that decide whether a citation is attached; the abstract: adjusting them alone restores or removes citations without changing answer accuracy
- Khan & Bhuyan, **Attributable Post-Rationalization in RAG Citations: A Controlled Reproduction and an RLVR Comparison**, arXiv:2609.23053 (2026) — **preprint**; a reproduction with an added control: about one citation in seven is unfaithful on Wikipedia-based questions, and search agents trained by RL with verifiable rewards do no better

**Evaluating RAG**
- Es et al., **Ragas: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation**, EACL 2024 System Demonstrations (arXiv:2309.15217) — automatic metrics that need no reference answers; the judge is an LLM
- Saad-Falcon et al., **ARES: An Automated Evaluation Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems**, NAACL 2024 (arXiv:2311.09476) — trains small judge models and corrects them with a few human annotations
- Ru et al., **RAGChecker: A Fine-grained Framework for Diagnosing Retrieval-Augmented Generation**, NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks (arXiv:2408.08067) — diagnoses retrieval and generation separately
- von Däniken et al., **The RAT: A Unified Bayesian Model for RAG Evaluation**, EMNLP 2026, pp. 15295–15310 (<https://aclanthology.org/2026.emnlp-main.664/>) — puts retrieval success, abstention and answer correctness in one Bayesian model; across 27 configurations, systems with equal marginal metrics can behave very differently
- Kucia & Gawlik, **Beyond Benchmark Scores: How Synthetic and Authentic Query Distributions Diverge in RAG Evaluation**, CIKM 2026 short paper (arXiv:2609.14579) — LLM-generated queries and authentic ones follow different distributions — evaluating on the former is biased

**Everything in the context, or retrieval**
- Li et al., **Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs? A Comprehensive Study and Hybrid Approach**, EMNLP 2024 industry track (arXiv:2407.16833) — planted in W5: with sufficient resources long context is better on average, and retrieval is far cheaper; the two give identical answers on over 60% of questions; Self-Route routes between them and cuts cost by 39–65%
- Xu et al., **Retrieval meets Long Context Large Language Models**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2310.03025) — an earlier comparison: retrieval helps even models with long contexts
- Li et al., **LaRA: Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Long-Context LLMs -- No Silver Bullet for LC or RAG Routing**, ICML 2025 (arXiv:2502.09977) — 2,326 test cases and eleven models: no universal winner; the answer depends on the model, the task and the retrieved chunks
- Gollapudi et al., **Can Language Models Actually Retrieve In-Context? Drowning in Documents at Million Token Scale**, NeurIPS 2026 (arXiv:2607.01538) — uses the context itself as the retriever over a whole corpus: as the corpus grows, irrelevant documents dominate the softmax denominator (attention dilution)
- Liu, **Length Is Cheap, Competition Is Not: Attention Predicts Context Rot in Retrieval**, arXiv:2611.04169 (2026) — **a single-author preprint** on open models of 0.5B–3B; the abstract: neutral filler up to 32k tokens costs nothing, while statements in the same format as the evidence cut accuracy to 0.16–0.33
- Banerjee et al., **The Bottleneck Is Retrieval, Not Reading: Diagnosing Evidence-Based Generation with RAG for Long Context Question Answering**, arXiv:2610.26951 (2026) — **preprint**; the abstract: similarity retrieval finds *some* relevant chunk far more reliably than *all* the chunks a question needs, and chunking discards document-level information
- Hong, Troynikov & Huber, **Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance**, a Chroma **technical report**, 2025-07 (<https://research.trychroma.com/context-rot>) — **a report from a vector-database company: not peer-reviewed, and the authors have an interest**; 18 models become less reliable on simple tasks as the input grows — the source of the term "context rot"
- Chan et al., **Don't Do RAG: When Cache-Augmented Generation is All You Need for Knowledge Tasks**, WWW 2025 short paper (arXiv:2412.15605) — when the knowledge base is small, put all of it in the context and precompute its KV cache, with no retrieval step
- Lu et al., **TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text**, EMNLP 2025 (arXiv:2410.07590) — precomputes the KV cache of every chunk offline; requires changes to masking and positions, and fine-tuning the model to cope
- Yao et al., **CacheBlend: Fast Large Language Model Serving for RAG with Cached Knowledge Fusion**, EuroSys 2025 (arXiv:2405.16444) — concatenates precomputed KV caches and recomputes only a small subset of tokens; the abstract: time to first token shorter by a factor of 2.2–3.3

**Who decides what to look up**
- Asai et al., **Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection**, ICLR 2024 oral (arXiv:2310.11511) — special tokens let the model decide whether to retrieve and critique its own output; the tokens are labelled in advance by a critic and trained in by SFT
- Jiang et al., **Active Retrieval Augmented Generation**, EMNLP 2023 (arXiv:2305.06983) — FLARE: decides when and what to retrieve while generating
- Trivedi et al., **Interleaving Retrieval with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Knowledge-Intensive Multi-Step Questions**, ACL 2023 (arXiv:2212.10509) — IRCoT: alternates one step of reasoning with one retrieval
- Jin et al., **Search-R1: Training LLMs to Reason and Leverage Search Engines with Reinforcement Learning**, COLM 2025 (arXiv:2503.09516) — **trains retrieval behaviour with the RL of W9**: the reward depends only on the final answer, and retrieved tokens are masked out of the loss; it returns next week
- Li et al., **Search-o1: Agentic Search-Enhanced Large Reasoning Models**, EMNLP 2025 (arXiv:2501.05366) — integrates search into the reasoning process of a reasoning model
- Edge et al., **From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization**, arXiv:2404.16130 (2024) — GraphRAG: an LLM first turns the corpus into a graph with hierarchical summaries, to answer questions that require aggregating over the whole corpus; **preprint**
- Xiang et al., **When to use Graphs in RAG: A Comprehensive Analysis for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation**, ICLR 2026 (arXiv:2506.05690) — the abstract: GraphRAG often underperforms plain RAG on real tasks; measures when the graph is worth it
- Sarthi et al., **RAPTOR: Recursive Abstractive Processing for Tree-Organized Retrieval**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2401.18059) — recursively summarises chunks into a tree, so that retrieval can draw on different levels
- Sen et al., **Is Grep All You Need? How Agent Harnesses Reshape Agentic Search**, arXiv:2605.15184 (2026) — **preprint**, 116 questions over conversational memory: inside an agent loop literal search mostly matches or beats vector retrieval, and results depend more on the harness

**Context engineering**
- Mei et al., **A Survey of Context Engineering for Large Language Models**, arXiv:2507.13334 (2025) — a 166-page overview; **a preprint, to be used as a map and not as assigned reading**
- Anthropic Applied AI team, **Effective context engineering for AI agents**, an Anthropic **engineering post**, 2025-09-29 (<https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents>) — **a company engineering post, not peer-reviewed**; treats context as a finite attention budget; compaction, notes kept outside the window, sub-agents, and loading data only when needed
- Zhang et al., **Agentic Context Engineering: Evolving Contexts for Self-Improving Language Models**, ICLR 2026 (arXiv:2510.04618) — adapts by changing the context instead of the weights; the abstract names two failures: repeated rewriting that erodes detail (context collapse) and dropping domain knowledge for the sake of brevity (brevity bias)
- Zhang, Kraska & Khattab, **Recursive Language Models**, NeurIPS 2026 (arXiv:2512.24601) — treats a very long prompt as an external environment that the model inspects with code and recursive calls to itself — a third path between long context and retrieval

**Retrieved text as an attack surface**
- Greshake et al., **Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection**, AISec 2023 (arXiv:2302.12173) — the source of indirect prompt injection: instructions hidden in content that will be retrieved; one of next week's main references
- Zou et al., **PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models**, USENIX Security 2025 (arXiv:2402.07867) — injecting a few texts into the knowledge base makes a chosen question receive a chosen answer

**Surveys, and work on local-language corpora**
- Deng et al., **Data-Centric Perspectives on Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey**, Findings of ACL 2026, pp. 1570–1588 (<https://aclanthology.org/2026.findings-acl.78/>) — an overview of data and benchmarks for agentic RAG; **the peer-reviewed survey to use for 2026**
- Lin et al., **A Comprehensive Survey on Reinforcement Learning-based Agentic Search: Foundations, Roles, Optimizations, Evaluations, and Applications**, arXiv:2510.16724 (2025) — an overview of search behaviour trained by RL; **preprint**
- Gao et al., **Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey**, arXiv:2312.10997 (2023) — the Naive / Advanced / Modular taxonomy; **dated, useful only as history; preprint**
- Lin et al., **A Preliminary Study of RAG for Taiwanese Historical Archives**, ROCLING 2025 (arXiv:2511.07445) — two Traditional Chinese historical archives from Taiwan; the abstract: integrating metadata early helps both retrieval and answers, while multi-hop and temporal questions remain hard

**Keywords only**
- IVF and product quantization (the other family of vector indexes): search for *product quantization for nearest neighbor search*, *inverted file index IVF-PQ*
- how to tokenise Chinese for BM25: search for *Chinese word segmentation information retrieval bigram indexing*
- prompt caching and the design of agent contexts (engineering posts by various companies): search for *prompt caching KV-cache hit rate agent context design*

> **Two gaps to state plainly in class** (as of November 2026). **For chunking and query rewriting there are now controlled studies and no consensus**: the three chunking comparisons of 2026 reach conclusions that do not agree, each tied to one retriever and one kind of corpus; this week replaces "best practice" by measurements on our own corpus. **The evaluation of RAG has no agreed standard**: no single metric has succeeded Ragas; progress has come in two directions — keeping part of the test data private (RTEB), and measuring the pipeline stage by stage (RAGChecker, RAT). Saying so is more useful than pretending a standard exists.
